title: Present simple and present continuous
tagline: Habits and facts, or right now and fixed plans — even when both talk about tomorrow.
exam: Speaking Part 1 — talking about your routine
why: Every notice, timetable and message in the exam mixes the present simple and the present continuous, and B1 Preliminary tests whether you can tell a routine from something happening now — or an already-arranged plan for tomorrow. The multiple-choice cloze and the note-taking listening both punish the classic mistake of putting -ing on a state verb like like or have. Get this contrast automatic and a big chunk of the grammar questions become easy.

hook.text: Science fair countdown. Sofia says: “Mateo, you always forget your notes!” Mateo: “Relax — I'm meeting Miss Vega after school to print them.” Sofia: “OK, because the fair starts at nine tomorrow.”
hook.ask: Look at the three verbs in bold. One is a routine, one is an arranged plan for later today, and one is a fixed timetable. Which is which, and why?

diagrams.title: Same action, different time

marks.label: she checks her phone every morning
marks.sub: present simple — a routine, again and again

marks.label: she's checking her phone right now

diagrams.caption: Present simple repeats across time like a stamp. Present continuous freezes one moment — now, or an already-arranged moment in the future.

diagrams.title: Build the sentence
diagrams.caption: The helper does/doesn't carries the S in the simple form; is/are carries the question in the continuous form.

rows.label: Use
cells: now, this week, temporary situations, future arrangements

rows.label: Time words
cells: always, usually, every day, on Mondays
now, at the moment, these days, tomorrow (arranged)

rows.label: Example
cells: We're leaving for Cusco on Friday.

use.point: Present simple for routines, facts and general truths

examples.text: Liam doesn't like maths, but he loves science.
examples.note: state verbs describe feelings, not actions happening now

use.point: Present simple for timetables and schedules

examples.text: The train to Arequipa leaves at six.
examples.note: a fixed timetable, even though it's about the future

examples.text: The science fair starts at nine tomorrow.
examples.note: school events work the same way as trains and buses

use.point: Present continuous for actions happening now or around now

examples.text: Sofia is printing the posters at this moment.
examples.note: happening right now, as we speak

examples.text: We're studying really hard this month because of the exams.
examples.note: around now — a temporary situation, not forever
a question about something happening now

use.point: Present continuous for future arrangements, and always + -ing for habits that annoy

examples.text: I'm meeting Liam at the stadium at five.
examples.note: an arranged plan — time and place already fixed

examples.text: Mateo and Nadia are visiting their grandparents next weekend.
examples.note: another fixed future plan, not a guess
always + -ing — a habit that annoys the speaker

watch_out.why: He/she/it takes an -s in the present simple.
Like is a state verb — it doesn't normally take the continuous form.

watch_out.wrong: Look, she sings very well right now.
watch_out.right: Look, she's singing very well right now.
watch_out.why: Something happening at this moment needs the continuous, not the simple.

watch_out.wrong: We are meeting Liam tomorrow at five, maybe.
watch_out.right: We're meeting Liam tomorrow at five.
watch_out.why: A real arrangement, with time and place fixed, doesn't need 'maybe' — that's a prediction, not an arrangement.

watch_out.wrong: Does she plays tennis on Saturdays?
watch_out.why: After does/doesn't, the verb goes back to its base form — no extra -s.

watch_out.wrong: The film starting at eight tonight.
watch_out.why: Timetables use the present simple, not the continuous, even when they talk about the future.

l1.why: Live as a permanent state uses the simple form, not the continuous, even though Spanish sometimes prefers estoy + gerundio.
Have meaning possess is a state verb — never in the continuous.

l1.wrong: She always loses the keys, that's normal.
l1.why: Spanish uses siempre + simple present for annoying habits; English prefers always + -ing to show it's irritating.

l1.es: El tren sale a las seis.
l1.wrong: The train is leaving at six, maybe.
l1.why: Spanish and English agree here: a timetable is present simple, not continuous.

remember.trick: Every day, add an -s. Right now? Use -ing!
remember.tip: If you can say 'always' or 'usually' before the verb, add -s for he/she/it. If you can point at it happening now, use am/is/are + -ing.

dialogue.title: The science fair countdown
dialogue.context: Sofia and Mateo are getting ready for tomorrow's school science fair; Liam and Miss Vega join to check the last details.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Mateo, the fair starts at nine. Where's your project?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Relax! I'm finishing the poster right now.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I need some help — Miss Vega, are you coming to check our stand?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes, I'm visiting every group before the doors open.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Mateo always leaves everything for the last minute!

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: That's not true — I'm working right now, look.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Great. Remember, the judges arrive at half past nine sharp.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Then we're meeting here at eight to set everything up.

items.sentence: The bus to Arequipa ___ at six.
items.why: a timetable uses the present simple

items.sentence: I ___ Sofia at the stadium at five tomorrow.
Mateo ___ chocolate — he eats it every day.
items.why: like/love are state verbs — no continuous form

items.sentence: Right now, Miss Vega ___ our science projects.
The science fair ___ tomorrow at nine.

can_do: I can talk about my routines and general facts with the present simple, remembering the -s for he/she/it.
I can describe what is happening right now, or around now, with the present continuous.
I can use the present continuous for arrangements already fixed, and the present simple for timetables.
summary: Present simple = routines, facts, timetables: add -s for he/she/it.
Present continuous = happening now, temporary situations, and fixed future arrangements.
State verbs (like, love, have, know, want) don't usually take the continuous form.
Always + -ing describes a habit that annoys the speaker, not a simple fact.
Timetables and scheduled events (trains, films, school fairs) use the present simple, even when they're about the future.
